stories.headline: New Ebola Treatment Trial Begins in Eastern Congo as Outbreak Surpasses 1,400 Cases
stories.summary:
Researchers began enrolling patients in a highly anticipated clinical trial in Bunia, eastern Congo, to test two potential treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which has infected more than 1,400 people and killed at least 438 since the current outbreak began. The World Health Organization announced Thursday that the first participant had been enrolled in the study, which is evaluating the antiviral remdesivir, an experimental antibody treatment called MBP134, and a combination of both. Unlike more common Ebola strains, the Bundibugyo virus has no approved specific treatment or vaccine.

The trial is being conducted at Bunia's Evangelical Medical Center in Ituri province and is a collaboration between Congo's national biomedical research institute, Oxford University, Antwerp's Institute of Tropical Medicine, and other international health groups, with WHO support. Survival will be tracked over 28 days following treatment. A second phase of the trial will expand to cover healthcare workers and high-risk contacts.

Health workers said the launch was marked by urgency rather than ceremony, as ambulances continued arriving at the treatment center during enrollment. Researchers estimate the trial could run three to six months depending on how the outbreak evolves. The loss of USAID funding has complicated international response efforts, according to public health officials.

For residents of Bunia, who have endured weeks of mounting fear and loss, the trial represents a rare source of hope. "I hope everything moves very quickly so that we can find relief," said one resident. Ebola survivor Gladys Munguro, recently discharged from a treatment center, said she witnessed fellow patients die while she recovered and urged swift progress in the research.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Intervened Directly with FIFA's Infantino Before Balogun Suspension Was Lifted
stories.summary:
President Trump personally called FIFA President Gianni Infantino to discuss U.S. striker Folarin Balogun's controversial red card and resulting suspension before the governing body reversed its decision on Sunday, a U.S. official told Axios. The reversal clears Balogun to play in Monday's knockout round match against Belgium, which would send the United States to its first World Cup quarterfinal since 2002 if the Americans win. FIFA's announcement of the suspension lift drew an immediate protest from Belgium, whose officials said they were "astonished" by the decision.

Direct presidential intervention in a FIFA disciplinary proceeding is highly unusual and raises questions about the influence of host-nation political pressure on tournament officiating. The episode illustrates the degree to which Trump has publicly aligned himself with the U.S. men's national team's World Cup run, which the U.S. is co-hosting. Critics argue that the reversal undermines confidence in FIFA's independence; supporters contend the original red card was wrong on the merits and the reversal was justified.

Balogun has been the breakout scorer of the Americans' strongest World Cup campaign in a generation. His absence would have significantly weakened the U.S. attack in the round of 16. Belgium's protest of the reinstatement decision is ongoing, and FIFA has not publicly detailed the basis for overturning the suspension.

stories.headline: White House Report Labels Smithsonian's American History Museum Leaders as Ideological 'Extremists'
stories.summary:
The White House Domestic Policy Council released a 162-page report on Independence Day accusing leaders of the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History of being "extreme" activists who are imposing their own ideology on the presentation of U.S. history. The report alleges the museum downplays the role of the nation's founders while emphasizing social justice themes, and charges that it "fails in the basic task of illuminating" American history for the public.

The report is part of the Trump administration's broader campaign to overhaul federally funded cultural and historic institutions in Washington. It follows earlier executive actions targeting Smithsonian programming and comes amid the administration's wider effort to reshape how American history is taught and commemorated on the 250th anniversary of the nation's founding.

Supporters of the administration's effort argue that taxpayer-funded institutions should present a more traditional, founder-centered account of American history rather than what they describe as politically motivated reinterpretations. Critics counter that the report represents political interference in scholarly and curatorial independence, and that museums' inclusion of social history reflects legitimate and well-established historical practice. The Smithsonian had not publicly responded to the report as of Sunday.

stories.headline: Update: Israel's Cabinet Votes to Defy Supreme Court in Unprecedented Constitutional Rupture
stories.summary:
Israel's cabinet voted unanimously on Sunday to openly defy a ruling by the country's Supreme Court, marking the first time in the nation's history that an Israeli government has formally committed to defying its highest judicial authority. The move dramatically escalates a long-running constitutional crisis over the power of the judiciary that has run in parallel with Israel's regional military conflicts.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has been locked in a bitter struggle with the Supreme Court over judicial oversight of government decisions, a fight that has divided Israeli society and drawn massive street protests. Previous confrontations had stopped short of outright defiance; Sunday's cabinet decision crosses that line explicitly.

The ruling sets a precedent with potentially sweeping consequences for Israeli democracy, as it removes a key check on executive power at a moment when the government is simultaneously managing a post-war environment in Gaza, ongoing tensions with Iran, and domestic political pressures. Legal experts in Israel warned the move could unravel foundational norms of the country's constitutional order.

Netanyahu, appearing on Fox News on Sunday, also pushed back against growing anti-Israel voices on the American right and addressed remarks by Vice President JD Vance, framing the United States and Israel as indispensable allies. He separately confirmed plans to meet with President Trump in Washington in the near future.

stories.headline: Republican Congressman Breaks With Trump, Urges 'Normalization' of Longtime Immigrants and Opposes Haitian Deportations
stories.summary:
Rep. Carlos Giménez (R-Fla.), a Cuban-American congressman from Miami, publicly broke with the Trump administration on Sunday, calling on the White House to "normalize" longtime undocumented immigrants and warning that deporting Haitians following the Supreme Court's ruling upholding the termination of Temporary Protected Status would be a "mistake."

"Haiti is a failed state," Giménez said, arguing that returning approximately 350,000 Haitians to a chaotic and dangerous country was untenable. His comments represent a significant crack in Republican unity on immigration at a moment when the administration is pressing forward aggressively with deportation efforts following a series of favorable court rulings.

The break is notable given Giménez's profile as a loyal Republican from a heavily Cuban-American district where hard-line immigration politics typically prevail. His call for a path to normalization — without specifying details — echoes arguments long made by Democrats and moderate Republicans but rarely voiced by members closely aligned with the Trump coalition.

The Trump administration has not publicly responded to Giménez's remarks. Democrats have pointed to the humanitarian risks of mass deportations to Haiti, while most Republicans have backed the administration's position that restoring immigration enforcement requires ending programs they see as executive overreach from the Biden era.

stories.headline: Obama Emerges as Potential Kingmaker as Democrats Begin Jockeying for 2028
stories.summary:
Barack Obama remains the most powerful and popular figure in the Democratic Party, and his de facto leadership role has been on prominent display over the past month as multiple potential 2028 presidential contenders have sought his guidance and endorsement, according to reporting from Axios and other outlets. Obama has not declared a preference among the emerging field but has been actively engaged with party leaders navigating an ideologically fractured coalition.

The jockeying comes against a backdrop of Democratic division, most visibly illustrated Sunday when Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow suspended her U.S. Senate campaign, narrowing that race to a two-person contest between progressive Abdul El-Sayed and centrist Rep. Haley Stevens — a microcosm of the broader ideological struggle playing out nationally. McMorrow's exit was seen as a significant reshaping of one of the most closely watched Senate primaries ahead of the August 4 vote.

The rise of democratic socialist candidates in recent primaries — including Zohran Mamdani's New York City mayoral win and Darializa Avila Chevalier's congressional primary upset — has intensified debate over the party's direction, with establishment figures warning of electability risks and progressives arguing the party must move left to energize its base. Speaker Johnson on Sunday noted the trend with concern, warning of "many Mamdanis" running for Congress.

Obama's potential kingmaker role is complicated by his reluctance to intervene in primaries and his effort to remain a unifying figure across factions. Party strategists say his eventual choice of whether — and whom — to endorse could prove decisive in shaping both the 2026 midterms and the 2028 presidential field.

stories.headline: Update: McMorrow Drops Out of Michigan Senate Race, Setting Up Two-Way Democratic Primary
stories.summary:
Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow announced Sunday that she is suspending her campaign for the U.S. Senate seat, a significant shakeup to one of the country's most closely watched Democratic primaries. McMorrow, who had sought to carve out a centrist lane, announced her withdrawal via a video posted to social media platform X, citing gratitude to supporters but not offering a specific reason for her exit.

Her departure narrows the race to a two-candidate contest between moderate Rep. Haley Stevens and progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who has been endorsed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and is tied to a pro-Hamas Arab-American political action committee — a fact that has drawn scrutiny from party leaders and opponents alike. The primary is scheduled for August 4.

Michigan is a Trump-won swing state that Democrats regard as critical to retaking the Senate majority. McMorrow had gained national prominence for a viral 2022 Senate floor speech but struggled to translate that attention into polling momentum in the race. Her exit forces Democratic voters and donors to consolidate around either the establishment-aligned Stevens or the insurgent El-Sayed ahead of a vote that could help define the ideological direction of the party heading into the midterms.

stories.headline: Update: FIFA Suspends Balogun Red Card, Clearing U.S. Star to Face Belgium; Belgium Protests Decision
stories.summary:
FIFA announced Sunday that it has suspended the one-game ban attached to U.S. forward Folarin Balogun's red card from the round-of-32 match against Bosnia and Herzegovina, clearing him to play in Monday's World Cup round-of-16 game against Belgium in Seattle. FIFA cited Article 27 of its Disciplinary Code, placing the suspension on a one-year probationary period — meaning if Balogun commits a similar infringement, the original ban will be reinstated alongside any new penalty.

The decision drew immediate backlash from the Royal Belgian Football Association, which called it "astonishing" and said it was "investigating all potential options," arguing the ruling is in "direct contradiction" of competition regulations explicitly reaffirmed to all participating nations in May. Belgium noted that every other red card issued at this World Cup had resulted in an automatic suspension, raising questions about consistency and the influence of political pressure on FIFA's administration of the tournament.

U.S. President Donald Trump publicly thanked FIFA on Truth Social, writing that the governing body had reversed "a great injustice." Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also called publicly for the decision to be reviewed. U.S. forward Christian Pulisic said the team learned of the reversal on a bus to training Sunday and that Balogun was "super happy." Balogun leads the Americans with three goals as the U.S. pursues its first World Cup quarterfinal berth since 2002.

stories.headline: Delta Plane Struck by Firework While Landing at Chicago's Midway Airport
stories.summary:
A Delta Air Lines Airbus A319 carrying 52 passengers and six crew members was struck by a firework during its descent into Chicago's Midway International Airport on Saturday night, amid the nation's 250th anniversary celebrations. The pilot reported the strike to air traffic control at approximately 200 feet of altitude, describing "a big bang." The aircraft landed safely and no injuries were reported among those on board.

Air traffic controllers had warned the crew before landing that multiple homes near the approach end of the runway were shooting off fireworks, and noted that the city had been informed but that it was unclear what action police would take. The Chicago Police Department told the BBC the plane was struck by "an unknown object" causing "minor paint damage." A post-landing inspection by Delta found no structural damage to the aircraft.

The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed the incident occurred around 20:30 local time and said an investigation has been opened. The incident highlights an ongoing safety tension between unregulated residential fireworks and airport approach corridors, particularly during major holiday celebrations. The FAA noted air traffic control was not providing direct services to the aircraft at the moment of the strike.

stories.headline: Update: Putin and Zelenskyy Hold Separate Calls With Trump as Ukraine Strikes Crimea
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy each held separate phone calls with U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday, discussing prospects for ending the war in Ukraine now in its fifth year. Zelenskyy said the two leaders agreed to continue talks in person at the upcoming NATO summit in Ankara, describing a "real prospect of ending this war" contingent on American determination. The Kremlin described Putin's call — lasting nearly 90 minutes and their fourth this year — as "constructive," with Trump reaffirming readiness to help achieve a quick cessation of hostilities and envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner prepared to visit Moscow.

Meanwhile, a Ukrainian strike on Russian-occupied Crimea killed one person and injured two others, according to Moscow-installed regional governor Sergei Aksyonov. Ukraine has intensified attacks on Crimean infrastructure in recent weeks as Kyiv seeks to isolate the peninsula and increase pressure on Moscow, whose battlefield advances have largely stalled.

The Kremlin accused Ukraine and European allies of "betting on prolonging, and even escalating the conflict," while Zelenskyy framed continued American engagement as decisive. The dual diplomatic contacts with Trump mark a notable moment in the peace process, though no formal negotiations or ceasefires have been announced and core disagreements over territory and security guarantees remain unresolved.

stories.headline: Mysterious Space Debris Spheres Wash Ashore on Australian Beach, Hazmat Teams Respond
stories.summary:
Six large solid spheres of apparent space debris washed up on Forrest Beach in northern Queensland, Australia, this weekend, prompting the Australian Space Agency to investigate their origin. Crews in protective suits were seen placing the objects into hazmat barrels under police guard amid concerns the spheres may contain hazardous substances, and authorities have established a 50-meter exclusion zone around the area.

Queensland's fire department urged any member of the public who encounters similar objects not to touch them, and to immediately contact emergency services. Online speculation suggests the spheres may be propellant tanks from spacecraft that could contain residual amounts of highly flammable or reactive substances such as hydrazine.

Australia has experienced similar incidents before — in 2023, India confirmed that a large metal dome found on a Western Australian beach was debris from one of its Polar Satellite Launch Vehicles. A comparable sphere was also discovered in remote Namibia in 2011, also believed to be a spacecraft fuel tank. The origin of the latest objects has not yet been confirmed.

stories.headline: Border Patrol Tops 21,000 Agents for First Time as Military and Law Enforcement Push Unconventional Recruitment
stories.summary:
U.S. Border Patrol has surpassed 21,000 agents for the first time in its history since its founding in 1924, the agency announced this week, as President Trump's administration pushes an intensified recruitment drive backed by billions in new funding. Trump signed legislation last summer mandating 3,000 new Border Patrol hires, and this month signed a broader $70 billion border security bill — including $26 billion specifically for Border Patrol — with much of the money designated for recruiting and retention.

The military and Border Patrol are deploying unconventional methods to attract new recruits, including co-sponsoring rodeo events like the Professional Bull Riders Space Cowboys event in Colorado Springs, where Space Force and Border Patrol recruiters set up booths alongside bull-riding competitions held to mark America's 250th anniversary. Event organizers say the overlap between rodeo culture — emphasizing hard work, integrity, and selflessness — and the values of military and law enforcement service makes these venues a natural fit.

Supporters of the expanded recruitment argue it reflects a necessary commitment to securing U.S. borders and fulfilling Trump's core campaign promises. Critics have raised concerns about the aggressive expansion of enforcement capacity and the normalization of Border Patrol's presence in civilian cultural spaces at a time when the agency's practices remain a subject of intense legal and political scrutiny. The new funding and staffing levels represent one of the most significant expansions of border enforcement infrastructure in the agency's history.

stories.headline: Update: Iran's New Leadership Takes Shape as Regime Undergoes Profound Transformation
stories.summary:
As Iran bids farewell to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei — killed in joint U.S.-Israeli airstrikes earlier this year — the country is undergoing its most significant political transformation since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. A fragile ceasefire with the U.S. and Israel more or less holds, but analysts warn the underlying conflicts remain entirely unresolved, and Iran's new leadership may prove more formidable than those it replaced.

The U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed last month at the Palace of Versailles, has been compared by some analysts to the Treaty of Versailles in its ambition and potential long-term consequences. Iran's nuclear program was significantly damaged but not destroyed, and the whereabouts of uranium stockpiles sufficient for roughly ten atomic weapons remain uncertain, with much believed buried beneath rubble near the Isfahan nuclear complex.

Iran's 'Axis of Resistance' proxy network suffered major setbacks during the war, yet the country has not collapsed as Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu predicted in January. Experts warn that the new faces leading Iran may take a more hardline or strategically sophisticated approach than their predecessors.

Johns Hopkins professor Vali Nasr told the BBC that the conflict is 'much more consequential and larger than we have given it credit for,' adding that major wars of this magnitude 'ultimately reorder the chess board' — and this one will do so for the entire Middle East.

stories.headline: Cargo Ship Reports Attack Off Yemen, Raising Red Sea Security Concerns
stories.summary:
A cargo vessel in the Red Sea reported coming under attack from armed assailants on Sunday, the latest in a series of security incidents threatening commercial shipping in the Middle East region. The attack adds to mounting concerns about maritime safety in waters already disrupted by ongoing regional instability.

The incident comes amid broader tensions in the Red Sea and surrounding waters, where Houthi forces in Yemen have previously targeted commercial and military vessels, severely disrupting global shipping lanes. Insurance premiums and rerouting costs for commercial shipping have remained elevated throughout the period of instability.

The attack underscores that despite the U.S.-Iran ceasefire signed last month, proxy forces and armed groups in the region continue to operate independently, posing ongoing risks to one of the world's most critical maritime corridors through which a significant share of global oil and consumer goods transit.

stories.headline: Messi Scores 20th World Cup Goal, Argentina Survives Cape Verde Scare
stories.summary:
Lionel Messi scored his 20th career World Cup goal on Friday, extending his all-time record and moving two goals clear of France's Kylian Mbappé on the tournament's all-time scoring list. The goal came in Argentina's 3-2 extra-time victory over heavy underdog Cape Verde, a result that was far closer than expected given Argentina's massive pre-match favoritism.

Messi, who now holds the record for goals in eight consecutive World Cup games — a streak stretching back to Argentina's 2022 title run — scored in the 29th minute on a precise near-post finish set up by defender Lisandro Martinez. He left the match with a visible welt on his forehead after a collision, though he said afterward that he was fine.

With seven goals in the current tournament, Messi leads Mbappé by one in the Golden Boot race. Mbappé scored his seventh of the tournament — his 19th World Cup goal all-time — in France's 1-0 victory over Paraguay the same day, setting up what is shaping up as a compelling individual scoring duel alongside the broader title competition.

stories.headline: Nigel Farage's Retreat From Public View Fuels Doubts About Reform UK's Direction
stories.summary:
Nigel Farage, the typically omnipresent leader of Reform UK, has gone conspicuously quiet in recent weeks, raising fresh questions within British political circles about the party's strategic direction and internal cohesion. The Sunday Times reported that Reform associate George Cottrell has been providing funds for Farage's security, drivers, staff, and accommodation, a disclosure that adds to scrutiny of the party's finances and leadership structure.

Reform UK surged in last year's UK general election, positioning itself as the dominant force on the British right, but critics have long questioned whether the party has the institutional depth to sustain its momentum beyond its charismatic leader. Farage's reduced public profile is being interpreted by some observers as a deliberate retrenchment and by others as a sign of internal trouble.

The development comes at a sensitive time for British right-wing politics, with Reform having displaced the Conservatives as the leading opposition force in several polls. How Farage navigates questions about party funding and his own public role is likely to be closely watched ahead of the next electoral cycle.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Strikes Down Trump's Birthright Citizenship Executive Order in 6-3 Ruling
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 to strike down President Trump's executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship, dealing a significant blow to one of the president's signature immigration priorities. The ruling upholds the longstanding interpretation of the 14th Amendment, which grants citizenship to virtually all persons born on U.S. soil regardless of their parents' immigration status.

The decision has drawn sharp reactions across party lines. Republicans who opposed the ruling argued Congress should pursue legislation targeting "birth tourism," with Rep. Byron Donalds calling it "a terrible decision." Some Democrats, including Rep. Ro Khanna, agreed that regulating immigration before entry is appropriate but argued that stripping citizenship from those born on U.S. soil would be unconstitutional.

Democrats broadly praised the outcome. Rep. Christian Menefee said the court "got it right" and called the 14th Amendment's meaning clear, while Rep. Seth Magaziner argued the Constitution's text is unambiguous and that changing it would require a constitutional amendment rather than an executive order.

The ruling represents one of the most consequential legal defeats for Trump's immigration agenda. Following the decision, ICE launched a surge of enforcement activity, making 10,000 arrests in five days. The White House has not yet announced whether it will pursue legislative alternatives to limit birthright citizenship.

stories.headline: Super Typhoon Bavi Bears Down on Guam with Catastrophic 160 mph Winds, Mass Evacuations Underway
stories.summary:
A super typhoon is bearing down on Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, with the U.S. National Weather Service warning of "catastrophic" damage. Typhoon Bavi is forecast to make landfall early Monday with sustained winds of up to 257 km/h (160 mph) and gusts reaching 207 mph, along with waves potentially reaching 35 feet and significant flooding from torrential rain.

Emergency evacuations are underway across both U.S. Pacific territories, with Guam opening five evacuation centers in schools for a population of approximately 170,000. Civil defense officials reported that at least one evacuation site reached maximum capacity Sunday afternoon. The National Weather Service warned the window for safe evacuation was rapidly closing and that winds "will pose a deadly threat to those venturing outside."

Bavi has been classified a super typhoon by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, a U.S. Navy unit, which predicts sustained winds of 150 knots upon landfall — the equivalent destructive potential of a Category 4 or 5 hurricane. Destructive conditions are expected to persist for eight to 10 hours before and after the storm's center passes over the islands Monday afternoon.

Scientists note the storm is part of a broader trend: Bavi will be the 11th Category 4 or 5 tropical cyclone to hit U.S. Pacific territory in the past decade, more than in the prior 57 years combined. Researchers attribute the increasing frequency and intensity of such storms to climate change and a strong El Niño pattern currently warming Pacific surface waters.

stories.headline: France Awaits Tuesday Verdict That Will Decide Whether Marine Le Pen Can Run for President
stories.summary:
France is bracing for a pivotal court ruling Tuesday as an appeals court in Paris prepares to deliver its verdict on Marine Le Pen's conviction for misuse of European parliamentary funds — a decision that will determine whether the nationalist frontrunner can compete in next year's presidential election. Le Pen, leader of the National Rally party and the leading candidate in current polls, was originally sentenced in March 2025 to two years of home detention and five years of ineligibility from public office, with the ineligibility portion declared immediately effective.

The appeal court will decide whether to confirm, overturn, or modify that sentence. Le Pen was found to have presided over a scheme in which RN staff in Paris were paid using EU parliamentary funds while posing as assistants in Brussels and Strasbourg. Her lawyers have sought acquittal, while the state advocate has again requested five years of ineligibility — which would definitively bar her from the race.

Legal observers are closely watching the possibility of an intermediate sentence. A shorter ineligibility term of two years, for instance, could theoretically allow her to stand, given the election's timing. If barred, RN's candidate would become 30-year-old Jordan Bardella, who polls suggest would also be competitive but whose youth and inexperience could prove liabilities during a campaign.

Le Pen has characterized her original conviction as a politically motivated attempt to prevent her from reaching the presidency, a claim her supporters have amplified. Critics and legal authorities maintain the case is a straightforward prosecution of documented financial misconduct. The ruling carries implications not only for French domestic politics but for the broader trajectory of European nationalist movements.

stories.headline: Chinese Underground Church Leader Released from Prison, Travels to U.S. After Trump Raised Case with Xi
stories.summary:
Jin Mingri, founder of Beijing's Zion Church and one of China's most prominent underground Christian leaders, has been released from prison and has traveled to Los Angeles, less than two months after President Trump directly raised his case with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a state visit to Beijing in May. Jin's family confirmed his arrival in the United States, calling his release "a miracle" and thanking both Trump and Xi for what they described as direct intervention.

Jin was imprisoned following overnight raids across China in October, in what Christian advocacy groups described as one of the harshest crackdowns on unregistered religious activity in China's modern history. Thirty church leaders were reported detained in that round of arrests. Jin's Zion Church, founded in 2007, had grown to approximately 10,000 members across 40 cities before being officially banned by the Chinese Communist Party in 2018 after it resisted government orders to install surveillance cameras on its Beijing property.

The Chinese foreign ministry has not publicly commented on Jin's release. U.S.-based rights group ChinaAid, which monitors religious persecution in China, confirmed the release while cautioning that "countless" other religious practitioners — including eight members of Zion Church — remain incarcerated. The Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, a Western legislative group, welcomed the news.

The release comes amid ongoing U.S.-China diplomatic engagement but does not signal a broader policy shift, according to observers. Trump also raised the case of pro-democracy Hong Kong media owner Jimmy Lai, sentenced to 20 years in prison, during his Beijing meetings. Lai remains imprisoned. China tightly regulates all religious practice and officially promotes state atheism, requiring worshippers to attend only government-sanctioned churches led by state-approved clergy.
